title: What is CTEM? The five stages explained
excerpt: Continuous Threat Exposure Management turns a yearly audit into a running practice. Here is how the five stages fit together.
body:
Most organisations still treat exposure management as an event. A test is commissioned, a report arrives some weeks later, the findings are worked through, and the cycle repeats next year. Continuous Threat Exposure Management, or CTEM, is the argument that this rhythm no longer matches how quickly an attack surface changes.

Gartner set out CTEM as five stages. They are worth understanding as a loop rather than a checklist, because the value comes from running them repeatedly and letting each pass sharpen the next.

Scoping

Scoping decides what you are actually defending. Not the full asset inventory, but the systems whose failure would hurt: the customer portal, the payment path, the identity provider, the build pipeline that can push code to all of them.

This is the stage teams most often rush, and it is the one that determines whether everything downstream is useful. A scope drawn around what is easy to scan produces a tidy report about the wrong systems. Scope is a business conversation before it is a technical one.

Discovery

Discovery finds what is in that scope, including the parts nobody registered. Forgotten staging environments, an S3 bucket from a campaign that ended two years ago, a subdomain pointing at a service that was decommissioned but never delisted.

Discovery reliably finds more than the asset register knows about. That gap is not an embarrassment, it is the point: you cannot test what you have not found, and attackers enumerate the same surface without needing permission.

Prioritisation

This is where CTEM departs most sharply from traditional vulnerability management. The question is not which findings carry the highest CVSS score, but which ones an attacker could realistically reach and chain together.

A critical rated flaw on an isolated internal host with no route to it may matter less than a medium rated one on an internet facing service that holds a session token. Severity is a property of the finding. Risk is a property of the finding plus its context.

A vulnerability that cannot be reached is a maintenance task. A vulnerability that can be reached and chained is an incident waiting for a date.

Validation

Validation asks whether the exposure is real and what it would actually cost. Three questions matter:

  • Can it be exploited in this environment, with the controls that are genuinely in place?
  • What does an attacker reach once they are through, and what can they chain from there?
  • Would the existing detection and response actually catch it?

This is the stage automation alone handles worst, and where a scanner's confidence is least trustworthy. Our agents surface candidates continuously, and a senior pentester confirms the ones that matter before they reach you. That combination is the reason our reports carry far fewer false positives than a raw scan.

Mobilisation

Mobilisation is the unglamorous stage that decides whether any of the previous four mattered. Findings have to become work that a team actually schedules, with an owner, a route to production and a way to confirm the fix held.

Programmes usually stall here, and rarely for technical reasons. The finding lands with a team that has no context for it, or no capacity, or no clear definition of done. Retesting closes that loop: a fix is not finished when it is deployed, it is finished when it has been tested again.

Why the loop matters more than the stages

Read as a checklist, CTEM looks like a rebranded vulnerability programme. Read as a loop, it is a different proposition. Each pass narrows the scope to what proved important, discovery gets faster as the inventory becomes real, and prioritisation improves because you have evidence from validation rather than a severity field.

The practical shift is one of tempo. An annual test tells you the state of your systems on one day of the year. A running loop tells you the state of your systems this week, which is the only version of the answer that stays true long enough to act on.
